lesson.title: For Loops and Accumulators: Building Up an Answer
lesson.objective: Read, predict and write for loops that use an accumulator to build up a result.
lesson.approachReason: The accumulator pattern is best learned by predicting what a loop produces before it is named, so every idea here is first met as a prediction to make and only then explained.

blocks.heading: What does this print?
blocks.prompt: A loop doesn't just repeat work — it can build up an answer as it goes. Before running this, make a prediction.
blocks.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 5, 2]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
blocks.explanation: total starts at 0 and each pass adds the next number: 0 + 3 = 3, 3 + 5 = 8, 8 + 2 = 10.
hints: Watch the variable total: it changes on every pass through the loop.
The print sits after the loop, so it runs once, with the value total ended up with.

options.feedback: total doesn't stay at 0 — every pass adds the next number into it.
That output would come from printing n inside the loop, not total after it.
15 comes from multiplying 3 × 5. The update line adds, so all three numbers go in.

blocks.heading: The accumulator pattern
blocks.body:
That pattern has a name: an accumulator. It is a variable created before the loop, changed on every pass, and read after the loop finishes.

There are always three parts, in this order: set up (total = 0), update inside the loop (total = total + n), and use after the loop (print(total)). The update line is the heart of it — it says "take what I already have and add this new item to it", so the variable grows instead of being replaced.

Put the set-up inside the loop and the accumulator is wiped clean on every pass, leaving you with only the last item.
blocks.example: total = total + n is so common that Python lets you write it as total += n. Same thing, fewer keystrokes.

blocks.heading: Step through the running total
blocks.prompt: Run this loop in your head, one line at a time, and watch what total holds after each line.
blocks.code:
total = 0
for n in [2, 5, 1]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
blocks.explanation: The accumulator keeps its value from one pass to the next — that is exactly what makes it an accumulator instead of a fresh value each time.
hints: On line 3, total appears on both sides: the right side is worked out first, then stored back into total.
After the first pass total is 2, so the next pass adds 5 to that 2 — not to 0.

trace.note: Create total and set it to 0.
Start the loop; n takes the first item, 2.
Add n to total and store the result back in total.
Loop again; n takes the next item, 5.
Add 5 to what total already holds.
Loop again; n takes the last item, 1.
The loop ends, so print runs once with the final value.

hints: Ask where each line has to sit: set up before, update inside, use after.
If a line runs on every pass, it cannot be the set-up.
blocks.retry: A counter is just an accumulator whose update is count = count + 1 — starting at 0 and growing by one per pass.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the shopping basket
blocks.problem: A basket holds prices = [4, 6, 3, 7]. Write a loop that builds the total cost, then prints the average price.

steps.title: Set up
steps.why: The accumulator must exist before the first pass, and it starts empty at 0.

steps.title: Loop
steps.text: Write for price in prices: and indent the body under it.
steps.why: Each pass, price becomes the next value in the list.

steps.title: Update
steps.text: Inside the loop write total = total + price.
steps.why: This adds the current price to whatever total already holds.

steps.title: Use it
steps.text: After the loop, unindented, write print(total).
steps.why: Only here does total hold the whole basket: 4 + 6 + 3 + 7 = 20.

steps.title: Average
steps.why: len(prices) is 4, so 20 / 4 = 5.0 — an ordinary expression that uses the accumulator.

blocks.answer: Final code: total = 0 / for price in prices: /     total = total + price / print(total) / print(total / len(prices)) — it prints 20 and then 5.0.

hints: Count how many times the indented print runs, and what total is at each moment.
The last line is not indented, so it sees the same total the loop finished with.
blocks.retry: Indentation is the clue: an indented print runs once per pass, an unindented print runs once when the loop is over.

hints: total does not start at 0 here, so read its starting value first.
Only the trays that go through the loop get added — the 100 is already inside total.
blocks.retry: The starting value is part of the answer: an accumulator beginning at 100 already contains the stock that was there before the loop.

blocks.heading: Your turn: what does this print?
blocks.prompt:
Read the loop carefully and work out the final value. Type just the number.

total = 1
for n in [2, 3, 4]:
    total = total * n
print(total)

traps.feedback: That's 2 + 3 + 4. The update line multiplies, so the numbers build a product, not a sum.
6 is total after only two passes (1 × 2 × 3). The loop makes a third pass with 4.

hints: Track total the way the trace did: write down its value after each pass.
After n = 2, total is 2. After n = 3, total is 6. What does the last pass do to 6?
blocks.solution: Trace it: total = 1, then 1 × 2 = 2, then 2 × 3 = 6, then 6 × 4 = 24, and print shows 24.

activities.title: Sort the lines of an accumulator loop
activities.prompt: Every accumulator loop has three phases. Drag each line of code into the phase where it belongs.
activities.reveal: Set the accumulator before the loop, change it on every pass, read it after the loop ends — that is the whole pattern.

activities.title: Order matters
activities.prompt:
This loop builds a word instead of a number. Before you run it, predict the output:

result = ""
for ch in "abc":
    result = ch + result
print(result)
activities.reveal: The same accumulate-on-every-pass idea works with any type: numbers add, strings join up, and the order inside the update line decides the final result.

options.feedback: That is what result = result + ch would give — here the new letter is put in front.
result is reassigned every pass, so the starting empty string is replaced on the first pass.
Nothing ever adds a space — only letters are joined.

questions.question: Maya has a list of songs called playlist and wants to know how many songs it holds. Which loop prints the correct count?
options:
count = 0
for song in playlist:
    count = count + 1
print(count)

for song in playlist:
    count = 0
    count = count + 1
print(count)
questions.correctAnswer:
count = 0
for song in playlist:
    count = count + 1
print(count)
questions.explanation: The counter is set to 0 before the loop, grows by one on every pass, and the final value is printed after the loop. The others reset the counter each pass, never print, or print a variable that was never created.

questions.question:
A student runs this code and watches the output:

total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
    print(total)
print("done:", total)

What appears on screen?
questions.explanation: The indented print runs on every pass, showing the running total 1, then 3, then 6. The unindented print runs once after the loop, when total still holds 6.

questions.question:
A bakery starts the day with 100 loaves in stock and then bakes three more trays:

total = 100
for tray in [10, 20, 30]:
    total = total + tray
print(total)

What is printed?
questions.explanation: The accumulator starts at 100 rather than 0, so it already contains the existing stock: 100 + 10 + 20 + 30 = 160.

problems: The lesson objective includes 'write' loops, but most learner practice is prediction, sorting, tracing and multiple-choice checks; there is no independent code-writing exercise.
The distractor feedback for the answer '15' in the first prediction is slightly confusing: it says 15 comes from multiplying 3 × 5, but the list also contains 2.
